source.title: Influence Scores at Scale for Efficient Language Data Sampling
source.authors: Nikhil Anand; Joshua Tan; M. Minakova

page_placements.theme: Example selection and sampling have conditional effects

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including appendices; no apparent cutoff or garbling affecting the relevant results.
record.tranche_reason: Tests influence-score-based training-data pruning in SNLI and a Japanese NLU stack, extending data-pruning results to language classification and a commercial-style setting. It does not test the claim versions’ specified interventions or measures.
record.gate_note: The paper reports held-out accuracy and error-rate outcomes after pruning examples by influence scores. It does not report the training error alongside these outcomes, so the training–test gap cannot be calculated. Cited findings from other studies are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study tests influence-score-based data pruning, but none of V1–V8. In particular, TracIn self-influence measures accumulated gradient products, not the inclusion-based change in own-label prediction probability defining memorization in V8. Random-label fitting, width, architecture, optimizer, batch-size, dropout and magnitude-aware sharpness comparisons are absent.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate: the authors present scalable, one-shot VoG sampling as a practical way to reduce language fine-tuning data while retaining broadly comparable performance. Their broad statements about no overall regressions require the qualification already included in the record: PDR-tail worsened significantly, and offline historical-data errors increased relative to full-data training.
record.recipe_differences: Uses example influence scores to prune fine-tuning data and measures downstream held-out performance; it does not test the claim versions’ architectural, optimizer, batch-size, regularization, width, sharpness, or memorization interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Sampling score and normalization; score timing for EL2N; pruning fraction; noisy versus clean data; domain distribution; the live user-study candidate combines DC VoG with NER-complexity scores.

fits_no_version.finding: Score-based pruning can preserve much of fine-tuned language-model performance, with outcomes depending on score, normalization, pruning fraction and noise. Removing 45% of class-normalized VoG-easy SNLI examples gives 85.04±0.20% accuracy versus 85.52±0.14% with all data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Influence-score-based selection can reduce language-classification fine-tuning data with limited accuracy loss under suitable sampling conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: At 52% historical-data pruning, dataset-normalized VoG produces smaller error increases than random sampling across all four offline metrics. The composite user-study system improves UER, has no significant overall PDR change and significantly worsens PDR-tail.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: VoG-based pruning can reduce historical NLU training data while retaining overall system performance, with residual offline error increases and risks for less frequent requests.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The paper does not report training error alongside held-out outcomes, so it cannot establish changes in the training–test gap. SNLI results are limited to one dataset and BERT models; in-house results are not readily reproducible, use fewer sampling techniques and prune sizes, and training data could not be strictly controlled across related runs. User-study per-domain comparisons were not hypothesis-tested.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant pruning result rows were omitted. Figure-based SNLI comparisons without exact textual values were not reconstructed as numeric rows; the corresponding textual summaries are recorded where available.

untested.parts: No comparison of fixed random-label fitting and natural-label held-out accuracy using the same architecture and recipe.
No width sweep beyond the width required for zero training error.
No convolutional versus fully connected image-classification comparison.
No adaptive-optimizer versus SGD comparison or tuning-budget experiment.
No batch-size comparison under fixed epoch budgets or adapted recipes.
Dropout is used but its effect is not experimentally compared.
No magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness measurement, gap-ranking comparison or correlation analysis.
No pruning based on the inclusion-induced change in own-label prediction probability. VoG, EL2N, forgetting, PVI and TracIn scores do not establish that the most memorized examples were removed.

record.verdict_notes: The mismatch with V8 is the selection measure, not missing training–test gaps: V8 requires held-out accuracy after memorization-based removal, without requiring a gap calculation. The record's blanket statement that training accuracy is unreported is incorrect: Appendix B.1 reports approximately 97% SNLI training accuracy after six epochs, although matched training results for the pruning conditions are not supplied.

versions.untested_parts: Does not compare fitting random labels with training on natural labels.
Does not sweep network width past the interpolation threshold.
Does not compare convolutional and fully connected architectures.
Does not compare adaptive optimizers with SGD for generalization.
Does not vary batch size or test large-batch generalization gaps.
Does not test dropout’s effect on held-out error.
Does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or compare it with generalization gaps.
Does not identify or remove examples based on memorization or their influence on predicting their own labels.
